profile.name: Gilbertese dancing
profile.tagline: Rhythmic fusion of song and movement from Kiribati.
profile.insight: Danced to singing and hand-beaten wooden boxes, Gilbertese dancing was targeted by missionaries who considered the cultural form scandalous.
profile.profile: Gilbertese dancing, also known as I-Kiribati dancing, is a traditional dance style of Kiribati reflecting influences associated with Melanesian and Polynesian expressive forms. It acts as a fusion of folk and ballad dance traditions accompanied by singing. Percussive rhythm is created by beating hand-held or upturned wooden boxes. Historically serving as a core element of cultural identity, it survived suppression attempts by European missionaries.
profile.profile_long:
Gilbertese dancing, also known as I-Kiribati dancing, represents a vital expression of cultural identity in Kiribati. Described as a characteristic style featuring elements shared across Melanesia and Polynesia, the tradition fuses folk and ballad dance forms. The performance relies intimately on vocal song accompaniment, creating a dialogue between movement and music. The primary rhythmic drive comes from percussive beating on upturned wooden boxes struck by hand.

During periods of European colonial contact, Christian missionaries sought to suppress Gilbertese dancing, viewing the traditional movements as scandalous. Despite these pressures, the dance maintained its place as a cornerstone of communal life and cultural self-expression. The formal structure of the dance links poetry, song, and movement in a cohesive storytelling medium.
